name: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (KCNT1)
aliases: malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy

clinicalPearls: A severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy of early infancy, most often caused by gain-of-function variants in KCNT1, which encodes the sodium-activated potassium channel Slack
The defining feature is near-continuous focal seizures that migrate independently between multiple cortical regions and between hemispheres, seen dramatically on video electroencephalography
Seizure onset is typically in the first six months of life, often within the first weeks, with rapidly escalating frequency
Development arrests or regresses with seizure onset, leading to profound impairment, acquired microcephaly, and loss of visual and social responsiveness
Other genes, including SCN2A, SCN1A, SCN8A, SLC12A5, and TBC1D24, can cause the same clinical syndrome, so it is genetically heterogeneous
Seizures are characteristically drug-resistant; quinidine has been trialled to target the KCNT1 gain-of-function channel but with inconsistent benefit and a need for cardiac monitoring
There is significant morbidity and mortality, including a raised risk of sudden unexpected death, so supportive multidisciplinary care and family counselling are central
reference.pathophysiology: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures is most commonly driven by gain-of-function variants in KCNT1, encoding the sodium-activated potassium channel Slack that shapes the slow afterhyperpolarisation and neuronal firing patterns. Enhanced channel activity disrupts the normal control of excitability and inhibitory balance, generating multiple independent seizure foci that migrate across the cortex. The relentless multifocal ictal activity impairs the developing brain, producing the characteristic developmental arrest and regression. Because the syndrome can also arise from sodium-channel and other genes, the migrating seizure phenotype reflects a final common pathway of severely disordered early network excitability.
additionalDifferentials: SCN2A, SCN1A, and SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
Structural or metabolic epilepsies of infancy
Ohtahara syndrome and early myoclonic encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Prolonged video electroencephalography to demonstrate migrating independent multifocal ictal patterns
Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing, with KCNT1 a priority target
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes and document acquired changes
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics
Electrocardiography and cardiac review before and during any quinidine trial
Developmental and growth monitoring including head circumference
redFlags: Near-continuous migrating seizures with developmental arrest in early infancy
Acquired microcephaly and loss of previously attained skills
Cardiac conduction changes during quinidine therapy
Features suggesting elevated sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
reference.prognosis: The syndrome generally carries a poor prognosis, with drug-resistant seizures, profound developmental impairment, and significant mortality including sudden unexpected death, though occasional milder courses are reported.
pitfalls: Expecting a reliable quinidine response when benefit is variable and requires cardiac monitoring
Assuming KCNT1 is the only cause and stopping the genetic workup
Overlooking treatable metabolic mimics early in the presentation
Neglecting family counselling about prognosis and sudden unexpected death risk
references: ILAE resources on epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medications are tried but seizures are characteristically drug-resistant, so rational combinations and early consideration of the ketogenic diet are used
A trial of quinidine to target the KCNT1 gain-of-function channel may be considered, with electrocardiographic and cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation, though benefit is inconsistent
Supportive care addressing feeding, respiratory and developmental needs with physiotherapy and occupational therapy input
Monitor development, growth and head circumference given the risk of regression and acquired microcephaly
Manage acute prolonged seizures and status epilepticus with an individualised rescue protocol
Coordinate care through paediatric epileptology and clinical genetics with confirmatory KCNT1 and broader gene-panel testing
Genetic counselling for the family alongside discussion of prognosis, sudden unexpected death risk and palliative support
